description: Team from Yogyakarta, Indonesia, building a web tool that shows, for any site and date near the Moon's south pole, whether a lander gets sunlight for power and a view of Earth for communication, using NASA LOLA terrain in 3D and Sun/Earth positions validated against JPL Horizons. I'm a full-stack web dev (Next.js, Three.js, Python). Looking for teammates in planetary science, UI/UX, video/storytelling, or Python/GIS. Like space and clear data? Join us!
summary:
LumaNav helps users explore where and when landing conditions may be favorable on the Moon.

Users can choose a launch site, target landing date, and flight route. LumaNav then works backward to estimate the launch time and ranks 15 candidate landing sites based on sunlight availability and direct visibility of Earth. Its analysis takes local lunar terrain into account, using elevation data from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) and astronomical positions calculated at 30-minute intervals.

The results can be explored through interactive 3D terrain, visibility timelines, a yearly landing calendar, and an Earth-to-Moon mission simulation. Each recommendation comes with a transparent score based on clearly defined criteria. Astronomical calculations are checked against NASA JPL Horizons, with a maximum angular difference of 0.0055°.

LumaNav uses deterministic calculations rather than an AI model, making its recommendations easier to inspect and understand.
details:
Live Application: https://lumanav-nasa.vercel.app/
Source Code: https://github.com/Davinsry/LumaNav
Demo Video: https://github.com/Davinsry/LumaNav/blob/main/docs/demo.mp4
Team: Flashover

What LumaNav Does

LumaNav brings lunar landing-site exploration, visibility analysis, and early mission planning into one interactive platform.

1. Plan a Mission

Users can select one of six launch pads, set a target landing date and time in UTC, and choose from three flight routes:

  • Fast: approximately 3 days
  • Standard: approximately 5 days
  • Low-energy: approximately 110 days

These duration estimates are informed by reference missions such as Apollo 11, Artemis I, and CAPSTONE. LumaNav works backward from the selected landing time to estimate when the mission should launch.

2. Explore Landing Recommendations

LumaNav evaluates 15 candidate landing sites across the lunar south pole, north pole, near side, and far side. It ranks the candidates and presents the top three for the selected mission scenario.

The evaluation considers conditions at touchdown and throughout the first seven days of surface operations. Users can inspect the score breakdown and preview each recommended location on the 3D lunar map.

3. Analyze the Landing Environment

For a selected site, users can explore:

  • Sunlight availability and direct Earth visibility.
  • A 30-day timeline showing how visibility conditions change.
  • A 360° terrain horizon profile with the paths of the Sun and Earth.
  • A yearly calendar highlighting potentially favorable landing days.
  • Lunar illumination maps.
  • Side-by-side comparisons of candidate sites and their estimated launch delays.

4. Visualize the Mission

Users can launch a 3D Earth-to-Moon mission simulation, following the major stages from liftoff and ascent to lunar orbit and touchdown at the selected coordinates.

After landing, a seven-day surface timelapse shows how sunlight and Earth visibility change at the site. A mission telemetry panel also provides information about the simulated flight.

How It Works

1. Lunar Terrain Data

LumaNav uses NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) LOLA elevation datasets:

  • LDEM_75S_240M and LDEM_75N_240M: approximately 240 m per pixel at the lunar poles.
  • LDEM_16: approximately 1.9 km per pixel across the Moon.

2. Terrain Horizon Analysis

From each candidate landing location, the system casts rays in 720 directions around the site, covering a full 360° horizon. The analysis extends up to 150 km and accounts for the Moon's curvature.

The highest terrain angle in each direction forms the local horizon profile. This helps determine whether surrounding terrain blocks the view of the Sun or Earth.

3. Sun and Earth Visibility

Sun and Earth positions are calculated every 30 minutes over a 30-day period using VSOP87 and the IAU lunar rotation model, including lunar libration.

The system considers the Sun visible when its apparent 0.53° disc is above the local terrain horizon. Earth is considered visible when its centre is above that horizon.

4. Landing-Site Scoring

Each candidate receives a deterministic score on a 0–100 scale. The scoring criteria are:

  • Sunlight available at touchdown: +20.
  • Earth visible at touchdown: +10.
  • Proportion of time with both sunlight and Earth visibility: +35.
  • Proportion of time with sunlight: +20.
  • Continuous sunlight at the beginning of surface operations: +15.

The weighted criteria are used to compare candidate sites over the first seven days after landing. The same inputs produce the same ranking.

5. Mission Planning and Simulation

The mission planner uses the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation to estimate velocity changes and propellant requirements based on typical delta-v values for each mission phase.

It also uses a Kepler transfer ellipse, an approximately 100 km polar lunar orbit, descent calculations toward the selected landing coordinates, and Earth's rotation to determine the launch pad's position.

These simplified models support early mission exploration and visualization; they are not a substitute for high-fidelity trajectory optimization.

Validation and Testing

LumaNav's astronomical calculations were compared with reference positions from NASA JPL Horizons across eight test epochs. The maximum angular difference was 0.0055°.

The project also includes automated tests covering:

  • Touchdown accuracy within 1 km of the selected target.
  • Physically reasonable flight speeds.
  • Launch-time calculations reaching the target landing time within one second.
  • Consistent rankings when the same inputs are used.
  • Correct orientation of lunar elevation maps, including far-side and equatorial cases.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Lunar landing conditions depend on more than geographic coordinates. Local terrain can block sunlight or obstruct the direct line of sight to Earth, and these conditions change over time.

LumaNav brings these factors together so users can compare candidate locations and landing dates without having to build a separate terrain and visibility analysis workflow.

The platform is intended to support:

  • Mission planners, who can compare candidate sites, landing times, and potential launch windows.
  • Lunar researchers, who can explore how terrain affects sunlight and Earth visibility.
  • Rover and lander teams, who can examine environmental conditions relevant to surface operations.
  • Space technology developers and students, who can explore lunar elevation data and astronomical visibility through an interactive tool.

LumaNav is an early-stage exploration and mission-planning support tool. It analyzes lighting and geometric line of sight; it does not guarantee landing safety, actual radio communication quality, or mission success. Its terrain resolution also varies by region, and its mission estimates use simplified models.

Future Development

Potential next steps include adding terrain slope analysis, lunar ice and temperature data from LRO Diviner, and more detailed solar-power estimates.

Technology Stack

  • JavaScript (ES Modules)
  • Vite
  • Three.js (WebGL)
  • astronomy-engine
  • Web Workers
  • Canvas 2D
  • Node.js test suite
  • Vercel for deployment
